core: the purpose and bounded contents of a project status report
dated actuals, comparison with an agreed reference, forecasts, risks, issues, decisions, and uncertainty
audience-appropriate detail and a deliberate reporting cadence
supporting: distinguishing a status report from the underlying tracking records
a hypothetical report that makes missing information and follow-up visible
outOfScope: designing a communications plan or selecting organization-specific report formats
detailed project tracking methods, earned-value calculations, risk-register design, or change-authority processes
organizational, procurement, employment, legal, financial, or certification advice

claims.claim: A status report communicates a selected, dated account of project conditions; for schedule information, reports can include actual status, actual-versus-planned progress, and forecasts.
The amount and regularity of reported schedule information should vary with stakeholder needs and project complexity, rather than follow one universal level of detail or cadence.
A useful report labels the status date and separates observations from forecasts, so readers can see what information is current and what is conditional.
A status label or color does not settle a project’s condition by itself; communicating status involves judgment and can be interpreted differently when criteria are unclear.

A concise general-education report can distinguish a risk (an uncertain possible future event), an issue (a current condition needing attention), and a decision or request; it should not imply that the report itself grants authority.
When data are incomplete, a more accurate report states the gap, its effect on confidence, and the next check instead of converting uncertainty into a definitive claim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The GAO guide describes detailed schedule reporting for public programs, while the PMI article is a practitioner reflection rather than a universal reporting standard.
positions: GAO describes reliable-schedule reporting, including actual, planned, and forecast data, and explains that audience and complexity affect reporting detail and regularity.
PMI’s article illustrates that a project status color can depend on interpretation and communication context.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses neither source as a mandated template. It teaches a transferable reporting discipline: identify the report date and reference, distinguish facts from forecasts, state material risks/issues/requests, adapt detail to the reader, and disclose uncertainty.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft defined status reporting only as a generic concept and did not teach report contents, audience, cadence, factual versus forecast information, uncertainty, or the distinction from tracking.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with original, source-grounded explanation of the status report as a communication product rather than a dashboard color or a substitute for project records.
Added bounded, transparent treatment of facts, forecasts, risks, issues, decisions, uncertainty, and audience needs without prescribing an organization-specific template or approval process.
Rebuilt all practice questions as four-option, evidence-supported questions with a balanced key distribution.
rightsIssues: GAO-16-89G is a U.S. government publication used for public-domain factual support; no prose, tables, dashboards, or templates are reproduced.
The PMI article is treated as reference-only. Its terms and scenario are not copied; all lesson prose and examples are original synthesis.

questionKeyCheck.method: Read every saved prompt, option set, correctIndex, explanation, and sourceIds after writing; then independently mapped correctIndex values to answer letters.
questionKeyCheck.result: Exactly five four-option questions cover recall, understanding, application, and analysis. Every A/B/C/D position occurs, including C and D; no position occurs more than twice.

sourceRecords.title: Schedule Assessment Guide: Best Practices for Project Schedules (GAO-16-89G)
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical existing Phase 3 source record reused exactly. Checked live, especially the Reporting and Communication discussion and Best Practice 9. Supports report audiences, reporting detail and regularity, actual/planned/forecast categories, status date, current progress, and the limits of stale or unsupported schedule status. The lesson uses original general-education prose only.

sourceRecords.title: How do you know the status of your project?
sourceRecords.notes: Checked live. A practitioner discussion illustrating that project status communication and the meaning of a color label require explicit context and judgment. Used only as a reference-only cross-check; no source wording, template, or scenario is adapted.
